lessons.title: Solvent Selection and Properties
lessons.body: Solvent extraction uses a liquid solvent to dissolve oil from oilseeds, leaving behind a dry meal. The most common solvent is food-grade hexane, a petroleum distillate. In Africa, hexane is imported and expensive, so you must use it carefully. Key properties: hexane boils at 68â69Â°C, which means it evaporates easily and can be recovered. It is highly flammable (flash point -22Â°C) and its vapours are heavier than air, so they pool in low areas. It is also a health hazard if inhaled. Other solvents like ethanol or isopropanol can be used, but they are less efficient and require more energy to recover. For small-scale operations in Africa, hexane is still the standard. You need solvent with low boiling point, low latent heat, low toxicity, and high oil solubility. Commercial hexane is a mixture of isomers with a boiling range of 60â70Â°C. Always buy food-grade hexane (not industrial grade) to avoid toxic impurities. Store it in sealed steel drums away from sparks, in a cool, ventilated shed. Never use petrol, kerosene, or other fuels as solventsâthey are toxic and leave harmful residues. Check the label for purity: at least 95% n-hexane. When you receive a drum, test its boiling point with a simple thermometer and distillation setup if possible. If it boils above 80Â°C, it contains heavy contaminants that will be hard to remove from oil. Keep records of solvent purchases and usage. In many African countries, hexane is taxed as a chemical, so budget for it. A typical small plant uses 2â5 litres of hexane per tonne of seed, but losses can be higher if equipment leaks. Proper selection and handling save money and lives.

lessons.title: Principles of Solvent Extraction
lessons.body: Solvent extraction works on the principle of dissolving oil in a solvent. Oilseeds first go through preparation: cleaning, cracking, dehulling, and flaking. Flaking is criticalâflakes should be 0.2â0.3 mm thick. Thin flakes rupture oil cells, allowing solvent to penetrate. The prepared flakes are then contacted with hexane in a countercurrent flow. In simple terms, fresh solvent meets the most exhausted flakes, while concentrated oil-rich solvent (called miscella) meets fresh flakes. This countercurrent design uses less solvent and extracts more oil. The main mechanisms are washing and diffusion. Washing removes oil from the surface; diffusion pulls oil from inside the flakes. Temperature matters: extraction is done at 50â60Â°C, just below hexaneâs boiling point, to reduce viscosity and improve flow. The ratio of solvent to flakes is typically 1:1 to 3:1 by weight. Contact time is 30â60 minutes in batch systems, or 20â30 minutes in continuous systems. After extraction, you get two streams: oil-rich miscella (20â30% oil) and wet meal (25â35% solvent). The miscella is distilled to evaporate hexane, leaving crude oil. The wet meal is desolventized to remove hexane, leaving meal for animal feed. Extraction efficiency should be 95â98% oil recovery. To test efficiency, take a sample of spent flakes and check residual oilâit should be less than 1%. If higher, adjust flake thickness, temperature, or solvent ratio. In Africa, many small plants use batch extractors because they are cheaper and easier to maintain. But continuous extractors save solvent and labour. Always monitor for solvent lossesâif you smell hexane, you are losing money and risking health. Use a simple flow meter or weigh your solvent tank daily. Keep extraction records: seed weight, solvent used, oil produced, and residual oil. This data helps you improve.

lessons.title: Batch and Continuous Extraction Systems
lessons.body: Batch extraction is the simplest system for small-scale African producers. You load flaked seed into a vessel, add hexane, stir, and drain the miscella. Then repeat with fresh solvent 2â3 times. A common batch extractor is a vertical cylindrical tank with a false bottom and a drain valve. You can build one from stainless steel or mild steel lined with epoxy. Capacity: 100â500 kg of flakes per batch. Cycle time: 1â2 hours. Labour: 2â3 workers. Solvent use: 3â5 litres per kg of oil extracted. Batch systems are cheap (USD 2,000â5,000) but labour-intensive and lose more solvent. Continuous extraction uses a series of connected extractors (e.g., a shallow-bed or deep-bed extractor) where flakes move continuously on a conveyor or through a rotary drum. Solvent flows countercurrently. Continuous systems handle 10â100 tonnes per day, recover 98% oil, and use only 1â2 litres of solvent per kg of oil. They cost USD 50,000â500,000, so they suit larger cooperatives or commercial plants. In Africa, countries like Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa have continuous plants for soybeans and sunflower. For a beginner, start with batch extraction. You can later upgrade to a continuous system by adding more extractor vessels in series. Key components for either system: a solvent tank, extractor, miscella tank, distillation unit, and condenser. For batch, you also need a stirrer and a pump. Always use explosion-proof motors and wiring. In continuous systems, the most common design is the Rotocel extractor (a rotating basket) or the Crown extractor (deep bed). You can find used equipment from Asia or Europe, but check for corrosion and worn seals. In Africa, local fabrication is possible: a welding shop can make a batch extractor from stainless steel. Ensure all welds are smooth and leak-free. Test with water before using hexane. Safety: never open an extractor while it contains hexane vapours. Purge with nitrogen or steam before maintenance.

lessons.title: Desolventizing and Toasting of Meal
lessons.body: After extraction, the wet meal contains 25â35% hexane. You must remove this solvent to make the meal safe for animal feed and to recover the hexane. This process is called desolventizing. The simplest method is heating the meal in a jacketed vessel with steam. Hexane evaporates at 68Â°C, so you heat the meal to 75â85Â°C for 30â60 minutes. But direct steam can also be injected to strip solvent. This is called desolventizer-toaster (DT) operation. In a DT, the meal moves through several trays. Steam heats the trays and also contacts the meal. The steam carries away hexane vapours to a condenser. After desolventizing, the meal still contains some water from steam. You then dry it to 10â12% moisture and cool it. Toasting is a critical step for meals like soybean, which contain anti-nutritional factors (trypsin inhibitors). Toasting at 100â110Â°C for 20â30 minutes destroys these factors. For groundnut or sunflower meal, toasting is less critical but still improves digestibility. In Africa, many small plants skip toasting, but that reduces meal value. You can build a simple DT from a vertical stack of trays with steam coils. Or use a rotary dryer with steam injection. The key is to monitor temperature and time. Use a thermometer in the meal outlet. If meal smells like hexane, you need more desolventizing. Test residual hexane by putting a sample in a sealed jar and smelling after 10 minutes. If you smell solvent, increase steam or time. The recovered hexane vapours go to a condenser and then to a solvent-water separator. The water layer is drained, and hexane is recycled. Typical desolventizing losses are 0.5â1.5 kg per tonne of meal. Keep records. In Africa, meal is a valuable product for poultry and cattle. Proper desolventizing and toasting can double its market price. Never feed meal with more than 0.1% residual hexaneâit is toxic to animals. Also, ensure the meal is not burnt; burnt meal is dark and has low protein digestibility. Use low-pressure steam (3â5 bar) and gentle agitation.

lessons.title: Solvent Recovery and Recycling
lessons.body: Solvent recovery is the heart of profitable solvent extraction. Hexane is expensive (USD 1.5â2.5 per litre in Africa). If you lose 5 litres per tonne of seed, that is USD 7.5â12.5 per tonneâa huge cost. So you must recover and recycle at least 99% of the solvent. Recovery happens in three places: from the miscella (oil-solvent mixture), from the wet meal (desolventizing), and from vents and leaks. The main recovery method is distillation. Miscella contains 20â30% oil and 70â80% hexane. You heat it in a distillation column or a simple pot still. Hexane boils at 68Â°C, so you heat to 80â90Â°C. The hexane vapour goes to a condenser (water-cooled) and becomes liquid hexane again. The oil left behind is crude oil, which still contains 100â500 ppm hexane. You can strip remaining hexane by steam injection under vacuum or by a second distillation. For small-scale plants, a batch distillation unit works: a kettle with a steam jacket, a condenser, and a receiving tank. You can build one for USD 1,000â3,000. In continuous plants, you use a rising film evaporator or a falling film evaporator. After distillation, the recovered hexane may contain water. You separate it in a decanterâhexane floats on water. Drain the water, and reuse the hexane. Check its purity: if it boils above 70Â°C, it has oil or water contamination. You can re-distill it. Also, recover hexane from the desolventizer vapours and from any vents by using a mineral oil scrubber or a chilled condenser. Keep your system sealed. Use gaskets, flanges, and welded pipes. Leaks are the biggest cause of solvent loss. Do a simple leak test: pressurize the system with air to 0.5 bar and spray soapy water on jointsâbubbles show leaks. Fix them immediately. In Africa, some plants lose 10â20 litres of hexane per tonne due to poor recovery. With good recovery, you can reduce that to 1â2 litres. That saves money and protects workers. Train your staff to check for hexane smells and to log solvent usage daily.

lessons.title: Safety and Environmental Controls in Solvent Extraction
lessons.body: Hexane is dangerous. It is highly flammable, and its vapours can explode if ignited. It is also a neurotoxinâinhaling it causes dizziness, headaches, and long-term nerve damage. In Africa, many small plants ignore safety, leading to fires and poisonings. You must follow strict controls. First, ventilation: work areas must have cross-ventilation and exhaust fans. Hexane vapours are heavier than air, so install exhausts at floor level. Use explosion-proof motors, switches, and lights. No open flames, no smoking, no sparks. Keep a dry powder fire extinguisher and a sand bucket nearby. Second, personal protective equipment (PPE): workers must wear chemical goggles, nitrile gloves, and respirators with organic vapour cartridges. Never use cotton glovesâthey soak up hexane. Third, spill control: keep absorbent materials (sand, sawdust) and a spill kit. If hexane spills, shut off ignition sources, ventilate, and absorb. Do not wash it into drainsâit is toxic to aquatic life. Fourth, health monitoring: rotate workers to limit exposure. The safe exposure limit is 500 ppm for 8 hours (OSHA), but aim for below 50 ppm. Use a simple gas detector or colourimetric tubes to check. Fifth, waste management: never dump hexane or oil sludge into rivers or on land. Collect waste solvent in sealed drums and send to a licensed recycler or incinerator. In many African countries, environmental agencies require an EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) for solvent plants. You must also manage the water from decantersâit contains traces of hexane. Treat it by air stripping or activated carbon before disposal. Sixth, emergency plan: post emergency numbers, train workers in first aid, and conduct fire drills. If someone inhales hexane, move them to fresh air and seek medical help. If hexane contacts skin, wash with soap and water. Never induce vomiting if swallowedâseek medical attention. Finally, keep records of incidents and near-misses. A safe plant is a profitable plant. Invest in safetyâit costs less than a fire or a lawsuit.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Solvent Extraction Technology in African Oil Milling

For African oil millers moving beyond manual presses and small expellers, solvent extraction is the step that turns oilseed cake into real money. A tonne of expeller cake still holds 6â12% residual oil; a properly run solvent plant can pull that down below 1%, recovering an extra 50â110 litres of crude oil per tonne while producing a higher-protein meal for the feed trade. This lesson is a working reference for operators, plant managers, and investors in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania, Zambia, and South Africa who need to run a solvent plant safely, profitably, and within environmental limits.

Solvent Selection for African Conditions

Commercial hexane remains the industry standard, but African operators must weigh cost, availability, and safety. Inland mills in Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Uganda often pay a premium for imported hexane, so some use locally refined petroleum fractions with wider boiling ranges. The trade-off is higher solvent loss and more energy in the distillation train.

Table 1: Key Properties of Common Extraction Solvents
Property Commercial Hexane Petroleum Ether Ethanol (Food-Grade)
Boiling range (Â°C) 63â69 40â60 78.3
Flash point (Â°C) â22 â40 13
Auto-ignition (Â°C) 225 ~200 363
Relative cost (Africa, 2024) High (imported) Medium MediumâHigh
Oil recovery efficiency 98â99% 96â98% 90â95%
Main constraint Explosion risk, import cost Very volatile, higher loss Energy-intensive recovery

Source: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 141 (1991); Anderson, A Primer on Oils Processing Technology, AOCS Press (1996); industry price surveys, West Africa, 2024.

Batch vs Continuous: What Fits Your Scale

Batch extractors (typically 1â10 tonnes per batch) suit small and medium mills where capital is tight and labour is affordable. Continuous systems (100â1,000 tonnes per day) dominate large operations in Nigeria, South Africa, and Egypt. The decision is business-driven: a 5 t/day batch plant may cost USD 80,000â150,000 installed, while a 100 t/day continuous plant runs USD 2â5 million. Payback depends on the spread between cake price and crude oil price â in 2024, that spread in West Africa was roughly USD 400â700 per tonne of oil recovered.

Table 2: Batch vs Continuous Extraction â African Context
Parameter Batch System Continuous System
Typical capacity 1â10 t/day 50â1,000 t/day
Capital cost (USD) 80kâ150k 2Mâ5M+
Solvent loss (kg/t seed) 4â8 1â3
Residual oil in meal 1.5â3% <1%
Labour requirement High Low (automated)
Best fit Rural SMEs, cooperatives Export-oriented processors

Source: FAO Bulletin 141 (1991); UNIDO Technology Transfer in the Vegetable Oil Industry (1990); market data from Nigerian and Kenyan processors, 2023â2024.

Desolventizing, Toasting, and Solvent Recovery

After extraction, the meal carries 25â35% solvent. The desolventizer-toaster (DT) uses direct steam to strip solvent, then indirect steam to toast the meal â raising protein digestibility and destroying anti-nutritional factors like trypsin inhibitors in soy. For African soy processors, proper toasting is non-negotiable: under-toasted meal fails feed mill quality tests, while over-toasted meal loses lysine and market value.

Solvent recovery is where profit leaks. A well-run plant loses 1â3 kg solvent per tonne of seed; a poorly maintained one loses 8â15 kg. At USD 1,200/tonne hexane, that difference is USD 6â18 per tonne of seed processed â enough to swing a mill from profit to loss. Key recovery points: condenser efficiency, condensate separation, mineral oil absorption, and steam stripping of the final oil.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â HEXANE IS EXPLOSIVE

Hexane vapour ignites at concentrations as low as 1.1% in air. All electrical equipment in the extraction building must be explosion-proof (ATEX or IECEx rated). No smoking, no open flames, no non-rated phones or torches. Static bonding and grounding on all vessels, pipes, and tanker unloading points is mandatory. In African plants, the most common causes of accidents are: (1) ungrounded solvent drums, (2) unrated lighting or motors, (3) inadequate ventilation in the extractor pit, and (4) untrained night-shift operators. Install continuous LEL (lower explosive limit) monitors with audible alarms, and enforce a permit-to-work system for hot work. A single drum of hexane can destroy a plant and kill workers â treat it accordingly.

Environmental Controls and African Regulatory Reality

Solvent-laden air and water are the main environmental issues. Condensers must achieve >95% recovery; vent gas should pass through a mineral-oil absorber or activated carbon bed before release. Wastewater from the DT and barometric condensers must be treated â hexane in effluent kills aquatic life and violates national discharge limits in Nigeria (NESREA), Kenya (NEMA), and South Africa (DWAF). Many African mills now use closed-loop cooling and zero-discharge designs to avoid fines and community complaints.

Also consider the meal market: solvent-extracted meal is a valuable feed ingredient, but only if residual solvent is below 500 ppm (typically <100 ppm in good plants). Buyers in the poultry and aquaculture sectors increasingly test for it. Your DT performance is therefore both a safety and a commercial issue.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Solvent quality: Verify boiling range 63â69Â°C and water content <0.1% before accepting any hexane delivery.
  2. Explosion-proof equipment: Confirm all motors, lights, switches, and instruments in the extraction zone carry ATEX/IECEx certification.
  3. Grounding and bonding: Test continuity on all vessels, pipes, and drum unloading points weekly; log results.
  4. LEL monitoring: Calibrate continuous gas detectors monthly; keep portable meters at the extractor and DT.
  5. Solvent loss tracking: Record daily solvent in vs. out; investigate any loss above 3 kg per tonne of seed.
  6. DT temperature: Monitor direct and indirect steam temperatures; target meal exit temp 105â115Â°C for soy, 100â110Â°C for groundnut.
  7. Effluent checks: Test wastewater for hexane monthly; ensure it meets NESREA/NEMA/DWAF limits before discharge.
  8. Operator training: Run quarterly refresher sessions on solvent handling, emergency shutdown, and fire response.

Further Reading

  • FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 141 â Small-scale Oil Extraction from Groundnuts and Copra (free, FAO)
  • FAO â Small-scale Oil Extraction from Groundnuts and Copra (full text, alternative link)
  • NESREA â National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (Nigeria)
  • NEMA â National Environment Management Authority (Kenya)
  • Department of Water and Sanitation (South Africa) â effluent and discharge standards

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Cooking Oil Production. This module is a practical reference for African agribusiness operators and does not replace site-specific engineering advice or local regulatory consultation.

quiz.q: What is the most common solvent used in cooking oil extraction?
quiz.explanation: Hexane is widely used because of its low boiling point and high oil solubility.

quiz.q: What is the boiling point of hexane?
quiz.explanation: Hexane boils at 68â69Â°C, which allows easy recovery by distillation.

quiz.q: Why is food-grade hexane preferred over industrial grade?
options: B) It has fewer toxic impurities
quiz.explanation: Food-grade hexane has fewer toxic impurities, ensuring safe oil for consumption.

quiz.q: What is the recommended flake thickness for solvent extraction?
quiz.explanation: Thin flakes (0.2â0.3 mm) rupture oil cells and allow better solvent penetration.

quiz.q: What is the typical extraction temperature for hexane?
quiz.explanation: Extraction is done at 50â60Â°C to reduce viscosity and improve flow without boiling the solvent.

quiz.q: What is miscella?
quiz.explanation: Miscella is the mixture of extracted oil and solvent.

quiz.q: What is the expected oil recovery efficiency in a well-run extraction plant?
quiz.explanation: Properly operated plants achieve 95â98% oil recovery.

quiz.q: In batch extraction, how many times is fresh solvent typically added?
quiz.explanation: Batch extraction usually involves 2â3 washes with fresh solvent to maximize oil removal.

quiz.q: What is a common continuous extractor design?
quiz.explanation: The Rotocel is a common continuous extractor that uses a rotating basket.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of continuous extraction over batch?
options: B) Less labour and solvent use
D) No need for solvent recovery
quiz.explanation: Continuous systems use less solvent and labour, and recover more oil.

quiz.q: What is desolventizing?
quiz.explanation: Desolventizing removes residual hexane from the meal after extraction.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of toasting meal?
quiz.explanation: Toasting destroys anti-nutritional factors like trypsin inhibitors in soybean meal.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for finished meal?
quiz.explanation: Meal should be dried to 10â12% moisture for safe storage.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe residual hexane in meal for animal feed?
quiz.explanation: Residual hexane above 0.1% is toxic to animals.

quiz.q: What is the main method for recovering hexane from miscella?
quiz.explanation: Distillation evaporates hexane, which is then condensed and reused.

quiz.q: Why is solvent recovery important?
quiz.explanation: Recovery saves money, protects worker health, and reduces pollution.

quiz.q: What is a simple leak test for a solvent system?
quiz.explanation: Pressurize with air and spray soapy water; bubbles indicate leaks.

quiz.q: What is the safe exposure limit for hexane over 8 hours?
quiz.explanation: OSHA sets the permissible exposure limit at 500 ppm for an 8-hour workday.

quiz.q: What type of gloves should be worn when handling hexane?
quiz.explanation: Nitrile gloves resist hexane; cotton or leather gloves absorb it.

quiz.q: Where should exhaust fans be installed in a hexane work area?
quiz.explanation: Hexane vapours are heavier than air, so exhausts must be at floor level.

quiz.q: What should you do if hexane spills?
quiz.explanation: Absorb spills with sand or sawdust, then dispose properly.

quiz.q: Why should you never dump hexane down a drain?
options: B) It is toxic to aquatic life
quiz.explanation: Hexane is toxic to aquatic life and can contaminate water sources.

quiz.q: What is the typical solvent loss in a well-run plant?
quiz.explanation: Good recovery can reduce solvent loss to 1â2 litres per tonne of seed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a decanter in solvent recovery?
quiz.explanation: A decanter separates immiscible hexane and water layers.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preparing oilseeds for solvent extraction?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt, stones, and foreign materials before further processing.

quiz.q: What is the ideal flake thickness for efficient extraction?
quiz.explanation: Flakes of 0.2â0.3 mm allow solvent to penetrate and extract oil efficiently.

quiz.q: What is the typical solvent-to-flake ratio in extraction?
quiz.explanation: A solvent-to-flake ratio of 1:1 to 3:1 by weight is typical.

quiz.q: What is the main safety hazard of hexane?
quiz.explanation: Hexane is highly flammable and its vapours can explode.

quiz.q: What type of fire extinguisher should be used for hexane fires?
quiz.explanation: Dry powder extinguishers are effective for flammable liquid fires.

quiz.q: What should be done with waste solvent?
options: B) Store in sealed drums for licensed disposal
quiz.explanation: Waste solvent must be stored safely and sent to a licensed recycler or incinerator.
